claims.text: Service-relevant mechanical loading at elevated and low temperatures induces localized atomic reordering at HEA grain boundaries.
Loading-induced grain-boundary reordering produces transient elemental segregation.
Loading-induced grain-boundary reordering can produce nanoscale phase changes.
Mechanical stress increases atomic mobility at grain boundaries.
Localized segregation or nanoscale phase formation reduces grain-boundary cohesion.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion lowers toughness and produces brittle failure.
The proposed HEA embrittlement mechanism differs from degradation caused by pre-existing intergranular segregation or precipitates in conventional alloys.
The tested HEA begins as a homogeneous, single-phase material.
The initial HEA has a uniform elemental distribution.
The initial HEA has no pre-existing grain-boundary segregation.
The initial HEA has no coarse precipitates.
A Ta-Nb-Hf-Zr-Ti-type alloy is a suitable example of the proposed compositionally complex HEA.
High-resolution TEM or atom-probe tomography can monitor grain-boundary chemical changes during applied loading in the proposed test.
Grain boundaries are preferential sites for stress-induced atomic reordering and segregation in the HEA.
The onset of brittle behavior will correlate with localized grain-boundary enrichment or incipient nanoprecipitate formation.
The loading-correlated grain-boundary chemical changes predicted for the HEA will be absent in the conventional-alloy baseline.
Toughness degradation in a conventional Ni-based superalloy baseline is linked to static grain-boundary segregation and precipitation.
The proposed mechanism applies under cyclic or continuous loading at elevated and cryogenic temperatures relevant to aerospace or energy service.
Other concurrent microstructural processes may contribute to any observed toughness degradation.
